questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman began enalapril for stage 1 hypertension 3 months ago. She now reports a persistent dry, nonproductive cough. She has no fever, sputum, or wheeze, and her chest examination and x-ray are normal. Which of the following best explains her symptom?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitor cough results from bradykinin accumulation, because ACE normally degrades bradykinin.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE degrades bradykinin, an inflammatory mediator, and ACE is expressed primarily in the lungs. Blocking ACE lets bradykinin and related molecules accumulate; their bronchoconstrictive effects produce the dry, hacking cough typical of ACE inhibitors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angiotensin I does build up behind the blocked enzyme, but it is an inactive precursor and is not what irritates the airways.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ACE inhibition lowers angiotensin II formation, so angiotensin II does not accumulate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperkalemia is a separate adverse effect of RAAS inhibition and does not cause cough.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Without fever, sputum, or abnormal imaging, and with onset after starting an ACE inhibitor, a drug effect is far more likely than infection.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with hypertension is started on losartan. Which of the following best describes how this drug lowers his blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocks ACE; less angiotensin II is formed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocks aldosterone receptors; more sodium is lost

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blocks Ang II receptors; Ang II is still formed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blocks renin; less angiotensin I is formed

explanation.summary: ARBs (-sartans) block angiotensin II receptors; angiotensin II is still produced but cannot act.
explanation.whyCorrect: ARBs act one step downstream of ACE inhibitors. Angiotensin II is still produced in the RAAS pathway, but its vascular receptors are blocked so it cannot cause vasoconstriction, and the net effect is a fall in blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This describes ACE inhibitors (the -pril drugs), which act one step upstream of losartan.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Losartan does not act on aldosterone receptors; it blocks angiotensin II receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting bradykinin degradation is a consequence of ACE inhibition; ARBs do not act on bradykinin breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This describes a renin inhibitor such as aliskiren, not a -sartan drug.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease takes lisinopril for hypertension. A potassium-sparing diuretic was added last month. Today his serum potassium is 6.1 mEq/L. Through which mechanism does the lisinopril contribute to this laboratory finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Efferent dilation, so more K+ is filtered

choices.label: B
choices.text: Less aldosterone, so less tubular K+ secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Less angiotensin I, so less K+ is excreted

choices.label: D
choices.text: More bradykinin, so K+ shifts out of cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: More renin, so more tubular K+ is reabsorbed

explanation.summary: RAAS inhibition lowers aldosterone, which reduces renal tubular potassium secretion and can cause hyperkalemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reducing angiotensin II and aldosterone decreases renal tubular potassium secretion, so potassium is retained. Risk is greatest in patients with CKD, diabetic kidney disease, or those on other potassium-retaining drugs such as potassium-sparing diuretics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Efferent dilation tends to lower GFR, and greater filtration would not raise serum potassium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ACE inhibitors do not lower angiotensin I (it accumulates); the potassium effect runs through aldosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bradykinin accumulation explains cough and angioedema, not the rise in potassium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin itself does not drive potassium reabsorption; the key step is the fall in aldosterone.

questions.stem: Five days after ramipril is started, a 72-year-old woman with heart failure has a rise in serum creatinine from 1.0 to 1.4 mg/dL. She is not taking any other new medication. Which change in renal hemodynamics best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: ACE-Is and ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, which can acutely lower GFR, especially in low-flow states such as heart failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Angiotensin II normally maintains GFR by constricting the efferent arteriole. Removing that effect dilates the efferent arteriole and can acutely decrease GFR, a form of prerenal AKI. The fall typically occurs within the first few days of therapy and is most likely in low-flow states such as dehydration or heart failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Afferent constriction is how NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow, not the action of an ACE inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A rise in GFR would lower creatinine, which is the opposite of what is seen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Efferent constriction is the normal action of angiotensin II and supports GFR; ACE inhibitors remove it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Obstruction is a postrenal process; this injury is hemodynamic and prerenal.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and proteinuria begins lisinopril. Four days later his estimated GFR is about 10% below baseline; his serum potassium is normal and he feels well. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add valsartan to deepen RAAS blockade

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change to half the dose starting today

choices.label: C
choices.text: Continue it and recheck in 7-10 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop it permanently as kidney injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to captopril to spare the kidney

explanation.summary: An initial modest fall in GFR on an ACE-I is acceptable; most patients return to baseline within 7-10 days.
explanation.whyCorrect: The drop in GFR usually occurs in the first few days and returns to normal in most patients within 7-10 days. Given the long-term benefit of these drugs in CKD and heart failure, an initial decrease can be accepted; the dose should be reduced or stopped only if GFR continues to fall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE-Is and ARBs should not be combined; dual blockade adds risk without benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dose reduction is reserved for a GFR that keeps falling, not a modest early dip.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A small early fall in GFR is expected and usually reverses; stopping would sacrifice the drug's long-term renal benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Captopril is also an ACE inhibitor and would have the same renal hemodynamic effect.

questions.stem: Two hours after taking benazepril, a 54-year-old man develops rapidly progressive swelling of his lips, tongue, and face. Which of the following is the most feared complication of this reaction?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema is rare but serious because airway obstruction can be fatal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Angioedema from bradykinin buildup commonly affects the upper airways, face, lips, and tongue. Airway obstruction is the most feared complication and can be fatal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AKI is a hemodynamic adverse effect of RAAS inhibitors and is not a complication of this swelling reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cough is a common, harmless bradykinin effect, not the dangerous consequence of this reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperkalemia is a separate electrolyte effect of RAAS inhibition, unrelated to facial and tongue swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Necrosis is not a feature of this reaction; the danger lies in where the swelling occurs.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old African American man is found to have stage 1 hypertension on repeated measurements. He has no other medical conditions and takes no medications. Which of the following is generally the most preferred first-line agent for him?

explanation.summary: For hypertension alone in an African American patient, a DHP calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine is generally preferred.
explanation.whyCorrect: African American patients have a 4.5 times greater risk of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema. When treating hypertension alone, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine is generally the most preferred first-line agent; an ARB trial with close monitoring is considered when comorbidities such as heart failure are present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Renin inhibitors see little clinical use and are not the preferred first-line choice here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: African American patients have a 4.5 times greater risk of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema, so an ACE-I is not preferred for hypertension alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Like other ACE inhibitors, lisinopril carries a higher angioedema risk in African American patients, making it less preferred for hypertension alone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An ARB trial with close monitoring is reserved for patients with comorbid conditions such as heart failure, not uncomplicated hypertension.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a blood pressure of 146/92 mm Hg and chronic kidney disease with persistently elevated urine albumin. Which of the following drug classes is most appropriate to lower her blood pressure and slow her kidney disease?

explanation.summary: ACE-Is and ARBs are first-line for CKD with proteinuria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Besides hypertension, ACE-Is and ARBs are first-line for CKD with proteinuria, post-MI, and heart failure. By dilating the efferent arteriole they reduce hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus and decrease albuminuria, slowing disease progression.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-blockers are used mainly for cardiovascular conditions and do not specifically reduce proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium channel blockers lower blood pressure but are not first-line for CKD with proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diuretics manage fluid balance but do not specifically reduce proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin inhibitors are rarely used; ACE-Is and ARBs are the first-line agents for proteinuric CKD.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with hypertension and heart failure takes lisinopril. His physician proposes adding valsartan to achieve 'more complete' blockade of the RAAS. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add it only after measuring a renin level

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add it only if his blood pressure stays high

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add it, but only with a potassium supplement

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add it: dual blockade further lowers mortality

choices.label: E
choices.text: Avoid it: added harm without proven benefit

explanation.summary: ACE-Is and ARBs should not be used together.
explanation.whyCorrect: Combining an ACE-I with an ARB adds hyperkalemia, AKI, and angioedema risk, and blocking the RAAS at multiple sites has never been shown to provide additional clinical benefit.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No laboratory value makes the ACE-I plus ARB combination appropriate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The combination should not be used regardless of blood pressure because of additive adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Potassium supplements would worsen the additive hyperkalemia risk of the combination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking the RAAS at multiple sites has never been shown to add clinical benefit.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman whose hypertension is controlled with losartan begins taking ibuprofen every day for knee osteoarthritis. Two weeks later her serum creatinine has risen sharply. Which combination of arteriolar effects best explains this change?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tubular toxicity with no vascular change

explanation.summary: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole while ACE-Is/ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, together greatly raising AKI risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE-Is and ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole, while NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole. Together they reduce renal blood flow and glomerular pressure, greatly increasing the risk of prerenal AKI, so chronic NSAID use should be avoided with these drugs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Losartan dilates rather than constricts the efferent arteriole by blocking angiotensin II.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This pattern would raise glomerular pressure and GFR, the opposite of what both drugs do.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The NSAID constricts, not dilates, the afferent arteriole.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This injury is hemodynamic (prerenal), arising from the opposing arteriolar effects of the two drugs.

questions.stem: Two patients with similar hypertension start therapy: one takes lisinopril and the other takes valsartan. Two weeks later, only the patient taking lisinopril has developed a persistent dry cough. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ACE-Is block renin release from the kidney

choices.label: B
choices.text: ACE-Is increase aldosterone and sodium excretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: ACE-Is inhibit the breakdown of bradykinin

choices.label: D
choices.text: ARBs also inhibit the breakdown of bradykinin

choices.label: E
choices.text: ARBs constrict the efferent arteriole instead

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors also block bradykinin breakdown, so bradykinin builds up and causes a dry cough; ARBs leave bradykinin metabolism alone.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE is the same enzyme as kininase II, which degrades bradykinin. Inhibiting it raises bradykinin and substance P in the airway, causing a dry cough in roughly 5-20% of patients. ARBs block the AT1 receptor downstream and don't affect bradykinin, so they are the usual switch for ACE-inhibitor cough. The two classes lower blood pressure to a similar degree.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE inhibitors act on the converting enzyme, not on renin release from juxtaglomerular cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ACE inhibitors lower, not raise, aldosterone, and this would not explain a cough.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ARBs do not affect bradykinin breakdown, which is why they rarely cause cough.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ARBs share the efferent-dilating effect of ACE inhibitors, and arteriolar tone would not cause a cough.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with chronic hypertension controlled on lisinopril tells you she has just learned she is 7 weeks pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate action regarding her lisinopril?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add valsartan and lower the lisinopril dose now

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue it and add a potassium supplement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Continue it, since it protects her kidneys

choices.label: D
choices.text: Discontinue it; the class is contraindicated

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to losartan, which is safe here

explanation.summary: ACE-Is and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnant women (and in bilateral renal artery stenosis), so the drug should be stopped and switching to an ARB is not an alternative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This adds dual RAAS blockade and keeps her on a contraindicated class.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Continuing the drug ignores the contraindication, and potassium supplements raise hyperkalemia risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kidney benefit does not override the contraindication of this class in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ARBs share the same contraindication in pregnancy as ACE inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman with newly diagnosed Type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on the usual first-line oral agent, a biguanide. Her fasting blood glucose, which had been driven largely by overnight glucose output, improves over the following weeks. Which of the following actions of this drug most directly explains the drop in her fasting glucose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of incretin receptors that suppress alpha-cell glucagon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of glucose reuptake in the renal proximal tubule

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct stimulation of insulin release from pancreatic beta cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slowing of gastric emptying that delays nutrient delivery to the gut

explanation.summary: Metformin lowers fasting glucose chiefly by decreasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metformin decreases hepatic glucose production by reducing gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Fasting glucose reflects overnight hepatic output, so this liver action is what lowers it. Metformin also improves peripheral insulin sensitivity and decreases intestinal glucose absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Incretin receptor activation with reduced glucagon secretion is the action of GLP-1 receptor agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking proximal tubular glucose reabsorption is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors, not metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metformin does not force insulin release; that is the action of insulin secretagogues and is why metformin has a low hypoglycemia risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Slowed gastric emptying is a GLP-1 receptor agonist effect and mainly blunts postprandial spikes.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: Investigators incubate isolated skeletal muscle cells with metformin and measure glucose entry into the cells, which rises well above control. The increase depends on an energy-sensing enzyme that monitors the AMP:ATP and ADP:ATP ratios. Activation of this enzyme leads to which of the following downstream events?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased expression of glucagon receptors on the myocyte

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased lipogenesis from the newly imported glucose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insertion of SGLT2 cotransporters into the sarcolemma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Movement of GLUT-4 transporters to the cell membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of insulin from granules stored in the muscle cell

explanation.summary: Metformin stimulates muscle AMPK, which drives GLUT-4 translocation, raising glucose uptake and lowering lipogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In skeletal muscle, metformin stimulates AMPK, the enzyme that monitors AMP:ATP and ADP:ATP ratios. AMPK activation moves GLUT-4 to the cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake and decreasing lipogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucagon receptor expression is not part of metformin's AMPK-driven mechanism in muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lecture states that metformin's GLUT-4 activation decreases lipogenesis, not increases it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SGLT2 is a renal proximal tubule transporter; metformin does not insert it into muscle membranes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscle cells do not store or secrete insulin; insulin comes from pancreatic beta cells.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity takes weekly semaglutide as his only glucose-lowering drug. He skips lunch during a long workday, and his fingerstick glucose that afternoon is 82 mg/dL without symptoms. Which of the following best explains why he did not become hypoglycemic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acts only on the liver to limit overnight glucose production

choices.label: B
choices.text: It lowers glucose only by blocking renal glucose reabsorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: It raises glucagon secretion from alpha cells during fasting

choices.label: D
choices.text: It releases less insulin as blood glucose falls

choices.label: E
choices.text: It speeds gastric emptying so food absorbs before glucose dips

explanation.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonists release insulin in a glucose-dependent manner, so they rarely cause hypoglycemia when used alone.
explanation.whyCorrect: GLP-1 receptor agonists increase insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner: they stimulate insulin release strongly when glucose is high and have little effect when glucose is low. This is why they rarely cause hypoglycemia when used without insulin or sulfonylureas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreasing hepatic glucose production is the main action of metformin, not semaglutide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal glucose excretion is the SGLT2 inhibitor mechanism; semaglutide acts on GLP-1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GLP-1 receptor agonists decrease, not increase, glucagon secretion from alpha cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GLP-1 receptor agonists slow gastric emptying; they do not speed it.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on dapagliflozin. A urinalysis two weeks later shows marked glycosuria although her serum glucose has improved. At which site does this drug act?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brush border of the terminal ileum

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors block glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule, increasing urinary glucose excretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin block the SGLT2 transporter in the proximal tubule, where filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed. Less glucose is reabsorbed, more is excreted in the urine, and serum glucose falls independent of insulin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pancreatic beta cells are the target of GLP-1 receptor agonists and insulin secretagogues, not SGLT2 inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The terminal ileum is where metformin interferes with vitamin B12 absorption; SGLT2 inhibitors do not act there.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Filtered glucose is reabsorbed through SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, not the collecting duct.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The liver is a main site of metformin action, where it decreases glucose production.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman began immediate-release metformin at a mid-range dose 6 days ago and now reports loose stools, bloating, and dyspepsia. She takes each dose on an empty stomach before breakfast and dinner. She wants to keep treating her diabetes. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add vitamin B12 to settle the bowel

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cut the dose and take it with meals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Double the dose to speed tolerance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop metformin and switch to insulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take it at bedtime on an empty stomach

explanation.summary: Metformin GI upset is managed by lowering the dose, titrating slowly, taking it with food, or using extended-release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastrointestinal upset is common when starting metformin and usually improves within 1-2 weeks. It can be mitigated by reducing a mid- or high-range dose, titrating slowly, taking it with food, or switching to an extended-release formulation, so therapy can continue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin B12 supplementation treats long-term B12 deficiency, not early GI upset.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Raising the dose would worsen dose-related GI effects; the strategy is to lower the dose and titrate slowly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stopping metformin is unnecessary; these common early GI effects can be mitigated while therapy continues.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Taking metformin on an empty stomach is the problem here; taking it with food is the recommended fix.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has taken metformin for Type 2 diabetes mellitus for 11 years. He reports burning and tingling in both feet and fatigue. Hemoglobin is 10.9 g/dL. Renal function is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his new findings?

explanation.summary: Long-term metformin can cause reversible vitamin B12 deficiency with anemia and neuropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-term metformin use is associated with reversible vitamin B12 deficiency, causing anemia and neuropathy. Metformin interferes with B12 absorption in the terminal ileum; about 7% of users are affected, and supplementation mitigates it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute pancreatitis is a rare GLP-1 receptor agonist adverse effect and presents with severe abdominal pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis is a rare adverse effect of SGLT2 inhibitors, not metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactic acidosis is an acute, potentially fatal acid-base disorder in high-risk patients; it does not cause gradual anemia and neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metformin carries a low risk of hypoglycemia, and hypoglycemia would not explain anemia.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman has taken metformin for 9 years. Her kidney function has slowly worsened, and today's estimated glomerular filtration rate is 26 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for her metformin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add vitamin B12 so the dose can be raised

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue it at a reduced dose with monitoring

choices.label: C
choices.text: Continue it at the current full dose unchanged

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop it because it is now contraindicated

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch it to an extended-release formulation

explanation.summary: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.
explanation.whyCorrect: An eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 is a contraindication to metformin because poor renal clearance of lactate greatly increases the risk of lactic acidosis. Continuing at a reduced dose is only an option in the 30-45 range for patients already tolerating it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B12 supplementation addresses B12 deficiency and has no bearing on the renal contraindication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced-dose continuation applies to an eGFR of 30-45 in a patient already tolerating metformin, not below 30.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Continuing full-dose metformin at an eGFR below 30 ignores a contraindication and raises lactic acidosis risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Extended-release metformin mitigates GI effects; it does not remove the renal contraindication.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: Researchers studying metformin in intestinal cell cultures find that treated cells release far more lactate into the medium than untreated cells. Which drug action at the cellular level best accounts for this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of the AMPK and GLUT-4 pathway in myocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of SGLT2-mediated glucose uptake at the brush border

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of the mitochondrial electron transport chain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interference with vitamin B12 uptake in the terminal ileum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of incretin release from enteroendocrine cells

explanation.summary: Metformin inhibits intestinal mitochondrial electron transport, shifting cells to anaerobic metabolism and lactate production.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the intestine, metformin inhibits mitochondrial electron transport. Cells then shift toward anaerobic glucose metabolism, which accumulates lactate. Normal kidneys clear this lactate, but impaired renal function predisposes to lactic acidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AMPK-driven GLUT-4 translocation is metformin's skeletal muscle mechanism; it increases glucose uptake rather than explaining intestinal lactate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SGLT2 blockade is the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors in the proximal tubule, not of metformin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired B12 absorption causes long-term B12 deficiency, not lactate production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Incretin signaling is mimicked by GLP-1 receptor agonists; it does not cause lactate accumulation.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity started liraglutide 3 months ago. He presents with 2 days of severe, constant epigastric pain that bores through to his back, with repeated vomiting. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Severe persistent abdominal pain radiating to the back on a GLP-1 receptor agonist suggests acute pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute pancreatitis is a rare but important adverse effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists. Patients are counseled to seek care for severe, persistent abdominal pain, especially if it radiates to the back or comes with vomiting.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis is linked to SGLT2 inhibitors, not liraglutide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genital mycotic infections are caused by SGLT2 inhibitor glucosuria and present with itching or discharge.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactic acidosis is a rare metformin adverse effect in high-risk patients and does not present as pain radiating to the back.
whyWrongByChoice.E: B12 deficiency develops with long-term metformin use and causes anemia and neuropathy, not acute abdominal pain.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with Type 2 diabetes mellitus taking empagliflozin has had a febrile viral illness with poor oral intake for 3 days. She presents with nausea, abdominal pain, and rapid deep breathing. Serum glucose is 188 mg/dL, arterial pH is 7.21 with low bicarbonate, and serum lactate is normal. Which of the following best describes her condition?

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with only modestly elevated glucose, especially during acute illness or fasting.
explanation.whyCorrect: SGLT2 inhibitors can rarely cause euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, in which ketoacidosis develops even though glucose is not extremely elevated. Risk rises with acute illness, prolonged fasting, dehydration, surgery, very low-carbohydrate intake, or low insulin availability.

whyWrongByChoice.B: She is not taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist, and the ketoacidosis is explained by her SGLT2 inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: She is not taking metformin, and her serum lactate is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Volume depletion alone would not produce a pH of 7.21 with low bicarbonate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her glucose is 188 mg/dL, and she is not taking a sulfonylurea.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes mellitus started canagliflozin 5 weeks ago. He now has redness, itching, and a white discharge under the foreskin. Which feature of this drug most directly predisposes him to this problem?

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitor glucosuria predisposes to genital mycotic infections such as candidal balanitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: SGLT2 inhibitors such as canagliflozin cause glucosuria, which increases the risk of genital mycotic infections such as candidal balanitis and vulvovaginal candidiasis. Good genital hygiene and early treatment reduce this risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactate accumulation relates to metformin and lactic acidosis, not genital infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Impaired B12 absorption is a long-term metformin effect that causes anemia and neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slowed gastric emptying is a GLP-1 receptor agonist effect causing GI symptoms, not genital infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Decreased glucagon secretion is a GLP-1 receptor agonist effect and does not predispose to genital infection.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and heart failure has had two hospital admissions for decompensation this year. He also has chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 41 mL/min/1.73 m2. He takes metformin at a reduced dose. Which of the following additions would best lower his risk of further heart failure hospitalization and slow his kidney disease?

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors are the high-yield choice to reduce heart failure hospitalization and slow CKD in Type 2 DM.
explanation.whyCorrect: Selected SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin reduce heart failure hospitalization and slow chronic kidney disease progression in patients with Type 2 DM. Current standards favor them in heart failure and CKD independent of metformin use or A1c.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Meglitinides are insulin secretagogues that can cause hypoglycemia and weight gain without heart or kidney protection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sulfonylureas can cause hypoglycemia and weight gain and offer no heart failure or kidney protection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Exenatide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist not among the agents with demonstrated cardiovascular benefit, and SGLT2 inhibitors are the high-yield choice for heart failure and CKD protection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: With an eGFR of 41, metformin should stay at a reduced dose; raising it increases lactic acidosis risk.

questions.topicName: Metformin, GLP-1 RA, and SGLT2 Inhibitors

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with cystitis due to Escherichia coli is prescribed sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. The sulfamethoxazole component structurally resembles a substrate that bacteria take in or produce. Which enzyme does the sulfamethoxazole component competitively inhibit?

explanation.summary: Sulfonamides mimic PABA and competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS).
explanation.whyCorrect: Sulfonamides are PABA mimics that act as competitive inhibitors of DHPS. DHPS normally combines PABA with pteridine to make dihydropteroic acid, a precursor of tetrahydrofolic acid (THF), so blocking it ultimately slows DNA, RNA and protein synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA gyrase is the target of a different antibiotic class; sulfonamides act earlier, in folate synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: RNA polymerase inhibition is the mechanism of other antibiotics; sulfonamides do not act on it directly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dihydrofolate reductase is the target of trimethoprim and pyrimethamine, the partner drugs, not of the sulfonamide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfonamides do not inhibit thymidylate synthase; their target is the enzyme that uses PABA.

questions.stem: A medical student compares the antibacterial action of sulfamethoxazole given by itself with that of sulfamethoxazole given together with trimethoprim. Which pairing correctly describes the effect on the organisms in each case?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Halts growth alone; kills bacteria when combined

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kills bacteria alone and when combined

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kills bacteria alone; antagonized when combined

choices.label: D
choices.text: Kills bacteria alone; halts growth when combined

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stops growth alone and when combined

explanation.summary: Sulfonamides alone are bacteriostatic; combined with TMP the effect becomes bactericidal.
explanation.whyCorrect: A sulfonamide by itself stops bacteria from growing and replicating without actively killing them (bacteriostatic). TMP is also bacteriostatic alone, but blocking two steps of the same pathway makes the SMX-TMP combination synergistically bactericidal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sulfonamides are not bactericidal on their own; they only stop growth and replication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The two drugs are synergistic, not antagonistic, and the sulfonamide alone does not kill bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the facts: the sulfonamide alone is bacteriostatic and the combination is bactericidal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adding TMP changes the effect: the combination is bactericidal, not merely bacteriostatic.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with an uncomplicated skin infection is given a two-drug combination tablet. One component is a folate antagonist that has stronger affinity for the bacterial form of its target than for the human form. Which reaction does this component block?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folic acid from diet to dihydropteroic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: PABA plus pteridine to dihydropteroic acid

explanation.summary: Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking conversion of DHF to THF.
explanation.whyCorrect: TMP (and pyrimethamine) inhibit dihydrofolate reductase, the enzyme converting dihydrofolic acid (DHF) to tetrahydrofolic acid (THF). TMP binds bacterial dihydrofolate reductase more strongly than the human enzyme.

whyWrongByChoice.B: TMP does not act at this step; it acts on the reductase that follows DHF formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is not a step in the bacterial pathway; dihydropteroic acid comes from PABA and pteridine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This step is catalyzed by DHPS, the target of the sulfonamide component, not of TMP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is the reverse of the reaction TMP blocks; the drug prevents THF from being formed.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student asks why a sulfonamide can block this synthetic pathway in bacteria without harming the patient's own cells. Which explanation is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human cells convert sulfonamides to inactive PABA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human cells lack DHPS and take up preformed folate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human cells rapidly pump sulfonamides back out

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human DHPS binds sulfonamides with low affinity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human reductase bypasses the blocked DHPS step

explanation.summary: Selective toxicity: mammals do not possess DHPS and use a folic acid transporter instead of making folate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mammals cannot make folic acid; they lack DHPS, the sulfonamide target, and instead import folate through a folic acid transporter. Most bacteria must synthesize folate themselves, so the drug selectively affects them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sulfonamides are not converted to PABA; selectivity comes from the absent drug target.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Efflux is a bacterial resistance mechanism, not the basis of human sparing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Humans do not possess DHPS at all; selectivity is not a matter of lower binding affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reductase acts after DHPS; humans are spared because they lack DHPS entirely and import folate.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation has a stable INR of 2.5. He is prescribed sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Five days later his INR is 5.8 and he has new bruising. Which mechanism best explains this change?

explanation.summary: SMX/TMP inhibits CYP2C9, slowing warfarin metabolism and raising INR and bleeding risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: SMX undergoes partial metabolism by CYP2C9 and SMX/TMP inhibits this enzyme. Warfarin is metabolized by CYP2C9, so its effect increases, the INR rises and bleeding risk goes up; close monitoring is advised.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enzyme induction would decrease warfarin effect and lower the INR.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Induction would speed warfarin metabolism and lower, not raise, the INR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The interaction responsible for raised INR with SMX/TMP involves CYP2C9, not CYP1A2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin is not a major substrate of CYP3A4, and the relevant SMX/TMP interaction is at CYP2C9.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension controlled by an ACE inhibitor is treated with sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for cystitis. Which laboratory abnormality is she at greatest risk of developing during therapy?

explanation.summary: SMX/TMP raises the risk of hyperkalemia, especially with ACEi/ARBs or NSAIDs and in the elderly.
explanation.whyCorrect: SMX/TMP increases the risk of hyperkalemia, and this risk is compounded by drugs such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs and NSAIDs. Hyperkalemia can be life-threatening in elderly patients and in patients with HIV, so these combinations require close monitoring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SMX/TMP does not lower albumin; sulfonamides bind albumin and can displace bilirubin from it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SMX/TMP does not typically lower potassium; the concern is the opposite.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyponatremia is not the electrolyte risk taught for SMX/TMP with ACE inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SMX/TMP does not affect calcium levels.

questions.stem: A pharmacist counsels a 24-year-old man starting sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim to drink at least 8 oz of water each time he takes a tablet. This advice is mainly intended to prevent which adverse effect?

explanation.summary: SMX/TMP can cause crystalluria; drinking at least 8 oz of water helps solubilize the drug.
explanation.whyCorrect: Use of SMX/TMP can result in crystalluria. Patients are told to drink at least 8 oz when they take the tablet because the fluid helps solubilize the drug.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolysis occurs in G6PD-deficient patients and is not prevented by fluid intake.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperkalemia is managed by monitoring and avoiding interacting drugs, not by drinking water with each dose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ototoxicity is not an adverse effect of SMX/TMP taught here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Photosensitivity is not the adverse effect this counseling addresses.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman who is 8 weeks pregnant has dysuria and urgency, and urine culture grows Escherichia coli. She asks for sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, which worked for a previous infection. Which explanation best supports choosing a different antibiotic for her now?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sulfonamide blocks fetal DHPS, halting nucleic acid synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sulfonamide crystals obstruct fetal renal tubules, risking agenesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sulfonamide displaces bilirubin, risking neonatal kernicterus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trimethoprim blocks fetal CYP2C9, causing drug accumulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trimethoprim impairs folate metabolism, risking neural tube defects

explanation.summary: TMP-SMX is avoided in the first trimester because TMP interferes with folate metabolism, risking neural tube defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the first trimester, TMP-SMX should be avoided because trimethoprim may interfere with folate metabolism and increase the risk of neural tube defects. The bilirubin-displacement concern applies to the last month of pregnancy, not to an 8-week gestation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Humans, including the fetus, do not possess DHPS, so this cannot be the mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Crystalluria is a maternal adverse effect and is not the reason the drug is avoided early in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bilirubin displacement and kernicterus are the concern in the last month of pregnancy, not at 8 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CYP2C9 inhibition matters for warfarin interactions, not for first-trimester fetal risk.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 37 weeks' gestation develops pyelonephritis. The team decides against sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim because of a specific risk to the newborn at this stage. Which neonatal complication are they most concerned about?

explanation.summary: Late in pregnancy, sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin, raising the neonate's risk of kernicterus.
explanation.whyCorrect: TMP-SMX should be avoided if possible in the last month of pregnancy because sulfonamides displace bilirubin bound to serum albumin. The rise in free unconjugated bilirubin could increase the risk of kernicterus in the neonate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gray baby syndrome is linked to a different antibiotic, not to sulfonamides.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neonatal hypoglycemia is not the late-pregnancy risk taught for TMP-SMX.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neural tube defects are the first-trimester concern; the neural tube has long since closed at 37 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tooth discoloration is associated with another antibiotic class, not sulfonamides.

questions.stem: A laboratory isolate of Escherichia coli that was previously inhibited by sulfamethoxazole becomes resistant after serial passage in the drug. Its DHPS gene sequence is unchanged, and drug uptake and efflux are normal. Which change in the isolate most likely accounts for its resistance?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methylation of the ribosomal binding site

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mutation in the DNA gyrase subunit

explanation.summary: Sulfonamide resistance can arise from increased PABA synthesis, which outcompetes the PABA-mimicking drug.
explanation.whyCorrect: The three primary mechanisms of sulfonamide resistance are alteration of DHPS, decreased uptake or increased efflux, and increased PABA synthesis. With DHPS and drug transport ruled out, overproduction of PABA, the natural substrate the drug competes with, is the remaining explanation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Less PABA would make the competitive inhibitor more effective, not less.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ribosomal changes affect protein synthesis inhibitors, not sulfonamides.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gyrase mutations affect a different drug class; sulfonamides act on folate synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-lactamases inactivate a different drug class and do not affect sulfonamides.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man taking sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim develops a spreading rash with blistering, painful oral erosions, and sloughing of skin over his trunk. Which action is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add folic acid supplementation to therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue the antibiotic with an antihistamine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the antibiotic dose by half

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to a topical sulfonamide product

explanation.summary: Any rash on a sulfonamide warrants stopping the drug, because SJS and TEN can be fatal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sulfonamides can rarely induce Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, severe skin reactions on a spectrum that can be fatal. If a patient taking a sulfonamide develops a rash, the offending medication should be discontinued.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid addresses folate deficiency, not a severe drug-induced skin reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Continuing the drug risks progression of a potentially fatal reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dose reduction still exposes the patient to the offending drug; it must be discontinued.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical sulfonamides are still sulfonamides and do not remove the offending drug.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is treated with sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection. Two days later he develops fatigue, dark urine, and scleral icterus, and hemoglobin has fallen from 14 to 9 g/dL. He had a similar episode after a different medication in childhood. Which underlying condition most likely predisposed him to this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dihydrofolate reductase deficiency of the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pyruvate kinase deficiency of red blood cells

explanation.summary: In G6PD deficiency, sulfonamide exposure can cause a rapid acute hemolytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rare reactions to sulfonamides occur in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, in whom exposure can trigger rapid acute hemolytic anemia, as seen here with falling hemoglobin, dark urine and jaundice after starting the drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is not a recognized predisposition; TMP inhibits human DHFR but that causes folate concerns, not acute hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is not the enzyme deficiency taught to predispose to sulfonamide-induced hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This deficiency affects thiopurine drug toxicity, not sulfonamide-induced hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This affects drug and bilirubin conjugation in newborns and does not explain acute hemolysis in an adult.
